Title: China Science and Technology 2020 ｜ How far is the ultimate energy for mankind?
Content: At the economic work conference of the CPC Central Committee at the end of 2020, the government deployed eight major tasks for the development of 2021.  This working meeting of top officials of the Communist Party of China not only listed "strengthening the national strategic scientific and technological strength" as the top priority for economic development next year, but also admitted to developing high technology through the advantages of the national system, "as soon as possible to solve a number of" neck jam "problems.  Looking back at 2020, China has a bright performance or national strategic deployment in the fields of lunar exploration, Mars exploration, satellite navigation, manned deep diving, quantum research, database technology replacement, international participation in nuclear fusion technology, and neutrino experiments and chip manufacturing.  What is the practical significance of scientific and technological research in these fields? What is China ’ s competitive advantage and realistic challenge?  Where is the next step?  The sun is the source of human energy, and the ultimate energy for human beings is still to be found inside the sun, which simulates the internal fusion reaction of the sun on the earth, that is, controlled nuclear fusion, and has also become the "artificial sun".  This is an incredible image of a solar “explosion ” released by NASA in 2018.  The Sun, the closest star to humans, is actually a supernuclear fusion reactor, with 600 million tons of hydrogen being converted into helium by fusion reactions every second. In the process, about 4.2 million tons of net energy is released into the universe, equivalent to 3.78 × 10 ^ 26 joules of energy.  The Earth obtained only 1.72 × 10 ^ 17 joules from it, equivalent to a net energy release of about 19 kilograms per second, creating a livable Earth ecosystem, which shows the power of nuclear fusion energy.  Compared with fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas, clean energy such as solar energy, and even cracking energy as nuclear energy, nuclear fusion energy has obvious advantages in energy density and environmental protection.  Take a power plant with 1 million kilowatts as an example, using coal, 2.5 million tons per year, requiring 250 trains of 100 sections to transport; using fuel, 110,000 barrels of oil per year, requiring 11 supertankers to transport; using a fission reactor, consuming 28 tons of uranium dioxide per year; using solar energy, requiring 5,000 acres of land and energy storage space; using a nuclear fusion reactor, requiring only 400 pounds of deuterium and 600 pounds. A ton of tritium, 1,300 pounds of lithium-6 can meet the need, and a small car can be transported.  At the same time, with coal, fuel oil as fuel, will produce tens of millions of tons of waste every year, human air pollution, greenhouse effect has long been intolerable; nuclear fission will produce 28 tons of highly radioactive waste, the current global nuclear waste treatment landfill as the main, the processing capacity has been saturated, these nuclear waste landfill tens of thousands of years after the human is still harmful; and nuclear fusion only produces 900 pounds of helium, zero environmental pollution.  More importantly, compared to coal, oil, natural gas and other fossil energy reserves are limited, solar energy, wind energy and other clean energy energy density is low, nuclear fusion energy has a very high energy density at the same time also has almost unlimited storage.  One liter of deuterium in seawater is equivalent to 300 liters of gasoline released by nuclear fusion, and there are more than 45 trillion tons of deuterium in seawater alone, releasing enough energy for humans to use for hundreds of millions of years.  Because of this, nuclear fusion energy is regarded as the "ultimate energy" of mankind. The so-called controlled nuclear fusion is actually simulating the nuclear fusion reaction inside the sun on Earth, so it is called the "artificial sun".  China's habitual confinement nuclear fusion experimental device "Shenguang" has so far developed to "Shenguang III", its ultimate goal is to achieve laser controlled nuclear fusion ignition.  (Shanghai Institute of Optics and Precision Machinery, Chinese Academy of Sciences) The US national ignition device and China's Shenguang controlled nuclear fusion technology are two major difficulties, one is how to trigger nuclear fusion, hydrogen bomb is formed by atomic bomb explosion high temperature and high pressure triggered fusion reaction, obviously can not be applied to controlled nuclear fusion; the first is how to control nuclear fusion under human control. Provide energy instead of releasing the power of destruction like a hydrogen bomb.  In addition, no material on Earth can withstand the high temperature and pressure required for nuclear fusion.  After several decades of development, there are currently two main branches of technology in the world controlled nuclear fusion research, one is the route of inertial confinement fusion (ICF), one is the route of magnetic confinement fusion (MCF).  The core of the device is that, through inertial or magnetic constraints, nuclear fusion occurs inside the device, while the entire device operates at a tolerable temperature and even ultra-low temperature.  For China, whether it is inertial restraint or magnetic restraint, there are research institutions that continue to exert efforts and walk on two legs.  The so-called inertial confinement, that is, the use of laser shock waves to make the fuel ball, which usually contains deuterium and tritium, reach extremely high temperature and pressure, and then "ignite" the nuclear fusion reaction inside the fuel ball.  Based on the way that the laser directly triggers the fusion reaction, the results of inertial confinement research can be used to produce pure fusion nuclear weapons, so most of the nuclear weapons research institutions in various countries are responsible for inertial confinement research, such as the United States Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL), China Institute of Engineering Physics, and there is very little exchange and cooperation between countries.  The National Ignition Facility (NIF), built by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States, is the world ’ s highest energy inertial confinement fusion experimental device. The building that houses the NIF device is 215 meters long and 120 meters wide, equivalent to three football fields, and can focus 2 million joules of energy through 192 laser beams to one point.  At present, NIF has successfully achieved "energy gain", that is, the energy generated by the fusion reaction exceeds the energy absorbed by the fuel for the first time, and also proves the feasibility of using a powerful pulse laser to "ignite" artificial thermonuclear fusion.  The "Shenguang-III" device, built in 2015 by the China Institute of Engineering Physics and the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Precision Machinery of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, is the world's second largest laser driver after the NIF in the United States.  In addition, Russia, France and others are building similar high-energy laser devices.  US National Ignition Facility Detailed explanation (click to view high-definition big picture): + 6 + 6 At present, the ICF technology route is still a long way ahead, compared with the magnetic confinement fusion route, the road ahead is much brighter, which can be called the field of modern nuclear fusion research.  Magnetic confinement fusion is currently focused on the Tokamak technology route, the Tokamak device was first developed by Igor of the Kurchatov Institute in the Soviet Union.  Igor Tamm, Andrei Sakharov, Lev Artsimovich and others invented it in the 1950s. In 1968, at the Third International Conference on Plasma Physics and Controlled Nuclear Fusion Research, the research results were first presented – plasma up to 1KeV was confined for a few milliseconds to shock the world, opening up magnetic confinement. The New World of Nuclear Fusion Research.  The center of the Tokamak device is an annular vacuum chamber, wrapped around a wire, and the inside of the Tokamak will generate a huge helical magnetic field when powered on, heating the plasma to a very high temperature to achieve the purpose of nuclear fusion.  After decades of research, the current Tokamak device has developed to the stage of superconducting Tokamak, and different from the ICF technical route, there has been continuous international cooperation and exchanges since the 1950s.  In the 1980s, the United States, the Soviet Union, the European Union, and Japan launched the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) construction plan, which was later stopped due to budget and other problems.  In 2006, China, the United States, Russia, India, Japan, South Korea and the European Union signed the ITER plan to build a superconducting Kamake-type fusion reactor in Cadarache, southern France, to explore the scientific and engineering feasibility of using fusion energy for peaceful purposes.  It is understood that ITER will become the world's first power station level fusion experimental reactor, which is an indispensable step to finally realize the commercialization of magnetic confinement fusion, which is also the largest international cooperation project that China has participated in as an equal partner for the first time.  According to the plan, China, the United States, Russia, India, Japan and South Korea each shoulder about 9% of the budget for a total of 65%, and the European Union as the equipment organizer provides the remaining 45% of the budget. title: Oxygen-generating experiment on Mars

passages.title: NASA's Mars rover receives oxygen from Mars' atmosphere for the first time
passages.passage: Mars Rover Perseverance for the first time was able to get oxygen from the atmosphere of Mars.  NASA launched it to the Red Planet in July 2020. — A growing number of discoveries of Perseverance, NASA ’ s newest six-wheeled work on the Martian surface, including the conversion of part of the thin, carbon-rich atmosphere into oxygen, — said in a statement of the space Agency.  The rover conducted the corresponding test on April 20, the 60th day since the landing of the mission to Mars.  The mission was carried out by a toaster-sized instrument aboard Perseverance called the Mars Oxygen In-situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE).  NASA explained that this discovery will help in the future to provide astronauts with air suitable for breathing.  Despite the fact that the atmosphere of the red planet is 96% carbon dioxide.  Also, the transformation of the local atmosphere with oxygen may allow in the future to produce fuel on Mars.  The agency noted that such achievements bring a person closer to landing on this planet.  The Perseverance rover was launched to Mars in July 2020 on the Atlas V rocket. The purpose of the mission is to search for traces of life in the Jezero crater, collect samples of rocks and sediments, and study the planet ’ s climate.  On February 22, the rocket landed on the surface of Mars.  In early March, the rover held its first test drive after landing.  The appearance of the “rainbow ” in the picture from Mars As part of the NASA Mars 2020 mission, the Mars Rover Perseverance took an unusual picture.  His lens got a rainbow, the appearance of which is impossible on Mars.  However, NASA has already officially denied the rainbow in the photo.  Its experts said that this is only a reflection of the sun, caught in the mechanism of the lens Hazcam Rover Perseverance.

passages.title: The expert assessed the prospects of creating a habitable atmosphere on Mars
passages.passage: Creating a habitable atmosphere on Mars will not work, but it is possible to produce oxygen there for a small team of researchers, scientists or colonists, said Vladimir Surdin, a senior researcher at the Sternberg State Astronomical Institute, commenting on the NASA report on the successful extraction of oxygen from the atmosphere of this planet.  NASA reported that the Mars Rover Perseverance for the first time extracted oxygen from the atmosphere of Mars.  It is expected that this technology in the future will help astronauts produce rocket fuel on this planet, as well as create a breathable atmosphere for them.  “Creating a habitable atmosphere on Mars, of course, will not work.  There are no resources for that.  But creating oxygen, for a small team of researchers, scientists or colonists on Mars, of course, is necessary.  Carrying oxygen from Earth is too expensive, you need to get it on Mars, ” says Surdin.  To get a small amount of oxygen on Mars has all the resources, the expert is sure.  The atmosphere of the planet is made up of carbon dioxide, which is carbon and oxygen associated with CO2.  In addition, Mars has water consisting of hydrogen and oxygen.  That is, in fact, oxygen on the planet is already there, but it is in a related form.  "Of course, it would be possible to break down water molecules - this is a process of hydrolysis, which in chemical terms, maybe, would be easier.  But there is very little water on Mars, and it lies in the polar caps, so it still needs to be reached.  And the atmosphere is everywhere, so humanity went a more difficult way, but so that at any point on the planet it would be possible to provide astronauts with oxygen.  That is, they decided to break down carbon dioxide molecules, ” the source said.  He emphasizes that the device that stands on the rover, rather cunning.  Nevertheless, it has proven its efficiency, which means it can be scaled - to send to Mars already larger vehicles of the same type.  They will be able to provide not only astronauts with oxygen for breathing, but also rockets that will be refueled with fuel - they need liquid oxygen as an oxidizer for the operation of engines.  Naturally, all this is quite expensive pleasure, as well as astronautics in general.  For example, the last rover that arrived on Mars in February is worth $3 billion.  This is a small car that weighs about a ton.  It is clear that any space flight is very expensive, but if there is a desire to explore a new planet, then you have to spend a lot, ” Surdin concluded.  Earlier, American scientists found that most of the water that previously covered the surface of Mars, did not escape into space, as it was believed until now, and is in the minerals that make up the rocks of the planet.

passages.title: Oxygen and hydrogen on Mars proposed to get from brine
passages.passage: Scientists have developed a method for producing oxygen and hydrogen from a liquid saline solution in Martian lakes using electrolysis.  A feature of the experiment was the use of lead-ruthenium oxide as an electrocatalyst for oxygen production.  The production of oxygen using such an installation was 25 times more energy efficient than in the case of MOXIE, launched to the Red Planet as part of the Mars 2020 mission, and the size and weight of the device for life support based on the described technology will be less than that of analogues.  The article was published in the journal PNAS.  Conditions on Mars are far from favorable for humans: the atmosphere is rarefied and 95 percent consists of carbon dioxide, and temperature changes exceed 100 degrees Celsius with an average temperature of minus 63 degrees.  Therefore, colonization of the Red Planet is impossible without the creation of a life support system that would be able to provide people with oxygen for breathing and fuel (for example, hydrogen) for energy supply and, ideally, return flight.  To solve the first problem, NASA created MOXIE (Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment) - an experimental installation for obtaining oxygen from atmospheric carbon dioxide by electrolysis.  To test the effectiveness of such a method in the field, the installation became part of the Mars Rover Perseverance, which was launched on July 30, 2020 as part of the Mars 2020 mission.  An alternative source of not only oxygen, but also hydrogen on Mars can be water, the first direct evidence of the existence of which on the red planet was obtained in 1971.  Particularly attractive for use in applications, however, would be the reserves of salt water, impurities in which would allow it to remain in a liquid state even at low temperature and pressure.  The first traces of such brine (liquid salt solution) with magnesium perchlorate as the main component were found on Mars in 2015, and in 2018, a reservoir with a diameter of about 20 kilometers was found under the polar ice of the planet, which could have been formed due to volcanic activity.  Later, planetary scientists confirmed that such lakes on Mars really exist and can be numerous.  Now Pralay Gayen (Pralay Gayen) from the University of Washington in St. Louis together with colleagues created an installation for obtaining oxygen and hydrogen from a saline solution close in composition and temperature to that in Martian lakes.  As a brine in the experiment, a solution of magnesium perchlorate in water with a concentration of 2.8 mol per liter was used, cooled to minus 36 degrees Celsius and blown by carbon dioxide (the latter played the role of the Martian atmosphere).  As an electrocatalyst for the production of oxygen, the scientists used lead-ruthenium oxide Pb2Ru2O7-δ, the effectiveness of which they previously showed for alkaline solutions.  The electrocatalyst for hydrogen production was platinum on activated carbon - the standard catalyst in this case, and a commercially produced anion-exchange membrane was used as a separator.  Installation diagram.  In the red region, oxygen is produced, in the blue - hydrogen.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS In the course of the study, scientists showed that lead-ruthenium oxide as an electrocatalyst is indeed several times more effective than the ruthenium oxide commonly used in such installations.  After the behavior of the created installation was studied in a wide range of temperatures from − 36 to 21 degrees Celsius and saw no radical fluctuations in the efficiency and rate of production.  The current output of the experimental installation was 70 percent, and the energy efficiency was in the range between 36 and 70 percent (depending on the voltage applied to the plates).  In addition, the installation was resistant to degradation of the catalyst: scientists were not able to find traces of ruthenium in the solution after 300-minute operation of the device.  The rate of production of oxygen (blue dots) and hydrogen (red dots), depending on the density of the cathode current.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS Also, the researchers compared the achieved rate of oxygen production with MOXIE values of 10-22 grams per hour: it turned out that with the same energy supply, the created installation produces 25 times more oxygen than the experiment on the Mars Rover “Perseverance ”.  To have the same rate of oxygen production as MOXIE, the device would have to have electrodes with an area of ​ ​ 28-62 square centimeters, and to ensure the vital activity of a sleeping and actively moving person, this parameter would have to be 375 and 1235 square centimeters, respectively.  At the same time, the mass and volume of the installation will be less than if you use the technology inherent in MOXIE.  Moreover, the developed method of obtaining oxygen does not require its subsequent purification, while during electrolysis in MOXIE, carbon monoxide is also produced, which must be filtered.  Dependence on the power consumption of the rate of oxygen production of the installation (blue line), as well as its capes and volume to ensure various modes of human life (black lines).  The blue dot is the power and rate of oxygen production at MOXIE.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS Previously, we talked about another method of obtaining oxygen from carbon dioxide in the Martian atmosphere (like MOXIE): scientists proposed to do this using low-temperature plasma.  And what is the role of the Mars Rover “Perseverance ” in addition to checking the method of oxygen production, you can read in our material“ Mars, there and back ”.  Nikita Kozyrev

passages.title: New technology will be able to produce hydrogen and oxygen from salty Martian water
passages.passage: In space launches, weight matters a lot, so the less we have to take with us, the better.  Now engineers at St. Louis University have developed a new electrolysis device that can convert very salty Martian water into breathable oxygen and hydrogen for fuel.  As you may remember from school, water electrolysis is the process of using electricity to break down water into its constituent hydrogen and oxygen atoms.  These gases can then be collected for use, so in theory electrolysis could be a way for astronauts to produce their own oxygen and hydrogen on the Red Planet.  The problem is that it doesn ’ t work well with brackish water, and that ’ s all you can find on Mars.  First, it is necessary to reduce the high salt content, which is a complex process in this inhospitable alien environment.  Therefore, for the new study, scientists have developed a new electrolysis system that can work with salt water in the extreme cold of the Martian atmosphere.  The key change is in two electrodes: the team created an anode from lead ruthenate pyrochlor and a cathode from platinum on the coal.  To test the new electrolyzer design, scientists modeled the Martian atmosphere, which required cooling to -36 ° C — and it worked.  The researchers say that at the same input power, the new electrolyzer produces 25 times more oxygen than MOXIE, the instrument aboard the Mars Rover Perseverance, which squeezes oxygen from carbon dioxide in the air.  While this technology has intriguing potential uses for astronauts, it ’ s worth remembering that water on Mars is a fairly rare commodity, so it ’ s probably better to use for drinking, although it also requires removing salt first.  Instead, the technology could first find application here on Earth.  "By demonstrating these electrolyzers in challenging Martian conditions, we also intend to deploy them in much milder conditions on Earth to use salt water to produce hydrogen and oxygen, for example by electrolysis of seawater," Pralai Gayen, a co-author of the study, said in a statement.  The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

passages.title: Mars Rover Perseverance successfully tested the device to extract oxygen from the Martian atmosphere
passages.passage: An experimental device called MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) was first tested on April 20, and this test was recognized as successful: for an hour of operation, the installation the size of a conventional toaster was able to produce more than 5 grams of oxygen, writes Newsru.  The atmosphere of Mars is almost 96% carbon dioxide (CO2).  The MOXIE unit is capable of converting this carbon dioxide into oxygen and carbon monoxide (CO, carbon monoxide), which is a by-product of the processing and is released back into the atmosphere.  The process of processing carbon dioxide occurs by electrolysis of solid oxides at a temperature of 800 degrees Celsius.  During operation, the device captures carbon dioxide, passes through a filter to remove dust and compresses it, providing pressure at ground level.  The gas then passes through a heated electrolysis cell, which consists of several layers of nickel alloy and ceramics.  Ceramic elements of the cell are able to conduct current at high temperature - they pass oxygen ions and trap carbon monoxide.  The outer surface of MOXIE is covered with a thin layer of gold.  This coating protects the MOXIE surface from heating, protecting the rover electronics located next to the instrument.  Future astronauts: breathe easier.  The MOXIE technology demonstration aboard @ NASAPersevere successfully extracted oxygen from the thin Martian atmosphere — a critical component for life support on the Red Planet and rocket fuel for the trip home. https: / / t.co / HOsguer. hYgkP pic.twitter.com / SwL0etf9Uu — NASA JPL (@ NASAJPL) April 21, 2021 The maximum estimated performance of MOXIE is up to 10 grams of oxygen per hour.  The test program includes at least nine more tests over two years.  These tests will be carried out under different conditions to assess the performance of the plant.  In the future, more large-scale oxygen production on Mars may come in handy for practical purposes.  First, oxygen is used as an oxidizing agent for rocket fuel.  For example, to launch a rocket with four astronauts from Mars to Earth requires about 7 tons of fuel and 25 tons of oxygen.  The ability to produce this amount of oxygen during the astronauts ’ stay on Mars will prevent this oxygen from being delivered from Earth – delivering a large and productive oxygen generator modeled on MOXIE would be a more practical solution.  Secondly, oxygen, which makes up 21% of the Earth's atmosphere, is needed for breathing - four astronauts will be enough one ton of oxygen for a year on Mars.  We will remind, the Rover Perseverance landed in the area of 45-kilometer crater Jezero, named after the village in Bosnia and Herzegovina.  This crater is located on the western edge of the Isis Plain (a giant impact crater north of the equator of Mars).  As scientists suggest, in ancient times in the area of ​ ​ the crater Ezero was a river delta, where organic matter and other potential traces of microorganisms that could have lived on Mars about 3 billion years ago could have been collected.  The crater itself was then filled with water and was a lake.

passages.title: How does NASA build a base with breathable air on Mars?
passages.passage: The purpose of writing this article is to understand how we can now prepare for human life on an alien planet, and to do so, Digital Trends spoke to two experts.  Michael Hackett, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Assad Abu Bakr, a NASA engineer, talk about how to keep astronauts alive on a planet that wants to take their lives.  The window of opportunity to send humans to the Red Planet has to pass some kind of necessary timeframe.  Because of the structure of the orbits of Earth and Mars, the easiest way to get from one planet to another is to use the Hohmann Transport Orbit, in which the spacecraft moves in an elliptical orbit and slowly and steadily pushes out.  Hackett explains, “It ’ s because of the way the planets move.  Earth is in orbit around Mars and is moving faster than Mars, so every once in a while they collide.  A year on Mars equals about two years on Earth. ”  So you have to go with the exact timing to launch astronauts to Mars.  Every Martian year, or every 26 months on Earth, is given a window of opportunity at which Mars is closest to Earth.  "So you have an optimal opportunity every 26 months to send a spacecraft to Mars through this orbit.  “So the plans for Mars are to send the infrastructure first, and then after 26 months, we ’ ll send the crew. ”  Sending infrastructure doesn ’ t just mean ensuring astronauts have access to air to breathe and food to eat.  It also means sending and building power plants, a habitat, rovers, and vehicles that will allow astronauts to leave Mars once the mission is complete.  Why is oxygen so important?  The first major problem to deal with when building a Martian base is the production of oxygen.  When you hear about producing oxygen on Mars, you ’ re probably thinking about the simplest human need: having air to breathe, and certainly not finding a way to produce a breathable atmosphere inside a confined habitat on Mars.  But the habitat will require, at least compared to other components of the project, very small amounts of oxygen.  By other components, we mean things like rocket propellants that lift astronauts off the surface of the planet.  Hackett explains, “We are trying to manufacture the drive prerequisites.  "We're not trying to make fuel, we're trying to get some of the necessary chemical reactions that we never think about on Earth."  On the ground, when you burn gasoline in your car ’ s engine, you use oxygen that weighs several times more than your fuel to cause that reaction.  The same is true of pieces of wood burning in the fireplace.  “But if you go somewhere where there is no free oxygen, you have to take oxygen with you. ”  Modern missiles have several liquid oxygen tanks that provide the final fuel and add a lot of weight to the entire payload.  “We ’ ll need about 30 tons of oxygen to get those astronauts off the surface and into orbit, and if we have to take those 30 tons of oxygen with us to Mars, the whole mission will be delayed for about a decade.  A much easier solution would be to send an empty tank there and fill it with oxygen. ”  Using what is available to produce oxygen on Mars, Hackett and his colleagues are working on a concept called In-situ Resource Utilization (ISRU).  Basically, it means using whatever is already found on Mars to build what we need.  They will have to experiment with a device called MOXIE, which, along with NASA's Endurance rover, successfully landed on Mars in February 2021.  MOXIE is essentially a miniature version of a much larger device that picks up carbon dioxide, which is found abundantly in the Martian atmosphere, and produces oxygen.  This device may seem complicated at first glance, but it ’ s actually similar to a very well-known technology on the planet.  According to Hackett, “MOXIE is very much like a fuel cell.  There is basically no difference between the two.  If you take a fuel cell and you reverse the two wires that have been wired into it, you have an electrification system.  This means that if the device is a fuel cell, you have a fuel and an oxidizer that deliver a stable molecule.  If you have carbon monoxide as fuel and oxygen, carbon dioxide is produced.  You also get electricity. ”  “Now, if you reverse that, you have to let in carbon dioxide and electricity, and what you get is carbon monoxide and oxygen.  That ’ s how we ’ ll solve the problem. ”  This seemingly simple idea is radical in that it addresses a problem that no one outside the aerospace community sees as a challenge: producing oxygen.  Hackett said, “Nobody wants to produce oxygen on Earth.  No one has a reason to do that.  Oxygen is everywhere. ”  How to build an oxygen machine?  Understanding the chemical rules of making an oxygen machine is one thing, and designing and implementing a version of it that fits inside a rover is another.  Abu Bakr, the MOXIE thermal engineer at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and who has been involved in the development of the MOXIE project from the beginning, explains how the experimental device was built and what obstacles the NASA lab team had to overcome.  He said: “The biggest challenge we ’ ve ever had is a little bit of energy.  The rover has a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, which is a nuclear source of electricity, so people think the rover relies on nuclear power, but that's not the case.  The rover is powered by batteries and has an atomic charger next to it. ”  This means that researchers need to be very careful about how much energy is being used to keep the battery from draining.  The entire Mars Endurance operates at only 110 watts, which is just a little more energy than it takes to light a light-bulb bulb.  As a result, a device like MOXIE has to operate with very small amounts of energy.  Simple knowledge but equipment design is only one aspect of trial and error – the other is to see if the idea works at all on Mars.  Even with concepts that work well on Earth, an alien environment can have unforeseen consequences, from the impact of the planet ’ s thin atmosphere on how heat is transferred to the depreciation of equipment in unexpected ways due to weaker gravity and unknown dust.  That ’ s why NASA engineers will soon be collecting MOXIE data to test its performance in Mars ’ true environment.  “In many ways, ” says Abu Bakr,“ MOXIE doesn ’ t really collect scientific data. ”  Compared to scientific equipment such as telescopes and spectrometers used to analyze rock samples, the data collected by MOXIE is relatively simple.  “What we get is almost like telemetry data in engineering.  We measure voltages and currents and temperatures, things like that.  This is our data, and the data is very small.  You can almost fit all of them in a floppy disk. ”  This means the team can get very quick feedback on whether the system is working properly – in just a few days.  Unlike other instruments on the endurance rover, which require weeks, months, or even years to analyze the data, MOXIE is a demonstration of practical performance rather than trial and error.  Abu Bakr said, “What we ’ re doing is not science, it ’ s technology.  We want to know whether the system works, and if we want to increase the scale in the future, what we need to do to make our goal work. ”  If MOXIE is successful, it will show how practical the ISRU principle is on Mars.  Then expanding the scale of the project and building a version of the machine on a real scale that produces oxygen at a much higher rate will be relatively easy; and the good news is that a larger version will appear more efficient and produce significant amounts of oxygen without requiring much energy. passages.title: Earth ’ s microbes should be sent to Mars.
passages.passage: Space agencies have taken a lot of precautions not to contaminate celestial bodies with terrestrial microbes, but some researchers believe sending Earth microbes to Mars could be beneficial because doing so could transform the Martian environment into a habitat for humans.  Researchers have recently said that Earth ’ s microbes should be sent to Mars for colonization so that the Red Planet becomes a suitable place for humans to live.  A recent study has shown that the spread of Earth ’ s microbes could trigger a change in the structure of the Red Planet and create an environment where humans can live.  Scientists have developed a process that involves screening promising microbes and leaving the most important on Mars.  The researchers' new paper shows that the release of human microbes is the beginning of the process of restructuring the Red Planet and creating an environment in which humans can inhabit.  Jose Lopez, a microbiologist and professor at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, USA, conducted the study with his colleagues.  They asked NASA and other space agencies to send microbes to Mars so they could change the planet ’ s unpredictable environment and create a habitable environment on Mars.  The main argument of the researchers is that preventing pollution is nearly impossible, but it can be done by doing some things, such as sending human microbes there.  According to the researchers, microorganisms are what made our planet habitable.  As we know, without beneficial microorganisms, life cannot exist.  More than four billion years ago, Earth was not a habitable place, but microbial life arose and evolved over time.  The findings were published in the FEMS Journal of Microbiology Ecology.

passages.title: Scientists have found organisms that can give rise to life on Mars
passages.passage: Scientists have found organisms that can give rise to life on Mars 16.02.2021, 14: 58 They are able to grow and multiply in the conditions of the red planet.  New experiments have shown that cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, can successfully grow in Martian atmospheric conditions.  Of course, a few more ingredients will be needed, but when humans get to Mars, they will be able to create life support systems based on cyanobacteria for the human habitat, writes nv.ua.  "Here we show that cyanobacteria can use the gases available in the Martian atmosphere, at low overall pressure, as a source of carbon and nitrogen," said astrobiologist Cyprien Verso from the University of Bremen in Germany.  "Under these conditions, cyanobacteria retained their ability to grow in water containing only Martian dust, and they could be used to feed other microbes.  This can help make long-term missions to Mars sustainable, ” the authors of the study believe.  All types of cyanobacteria produce oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis, and even today they are an invaluable source of it.  For several years, scientists have speculated whether we could use the ability of cyanobacteria to produce oxygen to live on Mars.  This will bring additional benefits.  The atmosphere of Mars consists mainly of carbon dioxide (95 percent) and nitrogen (3 percent), which are fixed by cyanobacteria, turning them into organic compounds and nutrients, respectively.  However, atmospheric pressure on Mars is a big problem.  The total pressure there is less than 1% of Earth ’ s — from 6 to 11 GPa: this is too small for the presence of liquid water, while the partial pressure of gaseous nitrogen — from 0.2 to 0.3 GPa — is not enough for their metabolism.  But recreating the atmosphere, like on Earth, would be too expensive: gases would have to be imported.  So the researchers were looking for a middle ground: an atmosphere close to Martian, which allows cyanobacteria to grow well.  The authors have developed a bioreactor called Atmos, which has an atmospheric pressure of about 10 percent of Earth ’ s, but uses only what can be found on Mars, albeit in inverted proportions: 96 percent nitrogen and 4 percent carbon dioxide.  The bioreactor also included water that can be obtained on Mars from melting ice, which in some places is abundant on the surface, and a simulator of Martian regolith, a mixture of minerals created here on Earth using only what can be found on Mars.  The team chose the type of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria that preliminary trials showed was most likely to thrive under these conditions, Anabaena sp.  PCC 7938, and tested it in a variety of conditions.  The researchers concluded that nitrogen-fixing, oxygen-producing cyanobacteria can be grown on Mars at low pressure under controlled conditions using exclusively local ingredients.  From cyanobacteria, sugar, amino acids and other nutrients can be obtained to feed other crops, which can then be used for other purposes, such as the production of medicines.  Atmos was designed to test whether cyanobacteria can be grown under certain atmospheric conditions rather than for maximum efficiency, and the parameters of the bioreactor will depend on many factors in the mission to Mars, including the payload and mission architecture.  However, now that the concept has been proven, the team can begin work on optimizing the bioreactor system that could one day save us life on Mars. Creating a sustainable atmosphere on Mars is a complex task that requires careful planning and execution. 
One of the key components of a sustainable atmosphere is the production of oxygen, which is essential for human life support [f23d0347-2a7a-42e3-92ae-041c694da975].

NASA's Mars rover, Perseverance, has successfully demonstrated the ability to extract oxygen from the Martian atmosphere using the Mars Oxygen In-situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE) [f23d0347-2a7a-42e3-92ae-041c694da975]. 
MOXIE is a toaster-sized instrument that converts carbon dioxide into oxygen and carbon monoxide [a9b637ed-3450-48ea-b997-51a387d2ede1]. 
The experiment was conducted on April 20, the 60th day since the landing of the mission to Mars [f23d0347-2a7a-42e3-92ae-041c694da975].

The MOXIE device uses electrolysis to break down carbon dioxide into oxygen and carbon monoxide [a9b637ed-3450-48ea-b997-51a387d2ede1]. 
The process involves capturing carbon dioxide, passing it through a filter to remove dust, and then compressing it to provide pressure at ground level [a9b637ed-3450-48ea-b997-51a387d2ede1]. 
The gas then passes through a heated electrolysis cell, which consists of several layers of nickel alloy and ceramics [a9b637ed-3450-48ea-b997-51a387d2ede1].

The MOXIE technology has the potential to provide astronauts with oxygen for breathing and fuel for rocket propulsion [a9b637ed-3450-48ea-b997-51a387d2ede1]. 
The device is capable of producing up to 10 grams of oxygen per hour, which is a significant improvement over previous oxygen-generating experiments [a9b637ed-3450-48ea-b997-51a387d2ede1].

However, creating a sustainable atmosphere on Mars is not just about producing oxygen. 
It also requires the production of other essential resources, such as water and food [736ae444-d7cc-4f58-8db8-ef94608744c8]. 
NASA is working on developing technologies to extract water from Martian soil and ice [736ae444-d7cc-4f58-8db8-ef94608744c8].

Title: NASA's Mars rover receives oxygen from Mars' atmosphere for the first time
Content: Mars Rover Perseverance for the first time was able to get oxygen from the atmosphere of Mars.  NASA launched it to the Red Planet in July 2020. — A growing number of discoveries of Perseverance, NASA ’ s newest six-wheeled work on the Martian surface, including the conversion of part of the thin, carbon-rich atmosphere into oxygen, — said in a statement of the space Agency.  The rover conducted the corresponding test on April 20, the 60th day since the landing of the mission to Mars.  The mission was carried out by a toaster-sized instrument aboard Perseverance called the Mars Oxygen In-situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE).  NASA explained that this discovery will help in the future to provide astronauts with air suitable for breathing.  Despite the fact that the atmosphere of the red planet is 96% carbon dioxide.  Also, the transformation of the local atmosphere with oxygen may allow in the future to produce fuel on Mars.  The agency noted that such achievements bring a person closer to landing on this planet.  The Perseverance rover was launched to Mars in July 2020 on the Atlas V rocket. The purpose of the mission is to search for traces of life in the Jezero crater, collect samples of rocks and sediments, and study the planet ’ s climate.  On February 22, the rocket landed on the surface of Mars.  In early March, the rover held its first test drive after landing.  The appearance of the “rainbow ” in the picture from Mars As part of the NASA Mars 2020 mission, the Mars Rover Perseverance took an unusual picture.  His lens got a rainbow, the appearance of which is impossible on Mars.  However, NASA has already officially denied the rainbow in the photo. Title: Oxygen and hydrogen on Mars proposed to get from brine
Content: Scientists have developed a method for producing oxygen and hydrogen from a liquid saline solution in Martian lakes using electrolysis.  A feature of the experiment was the use of lead-ruthenium oxide as an electrocatalyst for oxygen production.  The production of oxygen using such an installation was 25 times more energy efficient than in the case of MOXIE, launched to the Red Planet as part of the Mars 2020 mission, and the size and weight of the device for life support based on the described technology will be less than that of analogues.  The article was published in the journal PNAS.  Conditions on Mars are far from favorable for humans: the atmosphere is rarefied and 95 percent consists of carbon dioxide, and temperature changes exceed 100 degrees Celsius with an average temperature of minus 63 degrees.  Therefore, colonization of the Red Planet is impossible without the creation of a life support system that would be able to provide people with oxygen for breathing and fuel (for example, hydrogen) for energy supply and, ideally, return flight.  To solve the first problem, NASA created MOXIE (Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment) - an experimental installation for obtaining oxygen from atmospheric carbon dioxide by electrolysis.  To test the effectiveness of such a method in the field, the installation became part of the Mars Rover Perseverance, which was launched on July 30, 2020 as part of the Mars 2020 mission.  An alternative source of not only oxygen, but also hydrogen on Mars can be water, the first direct evidence of the existence of which on the red planet was obtained in 1971.  Particularly attractive for use in applications, however, would be the reserves of salt water, impurities in which would allow it to remain in a liquid state even at low temperature and pressure.  The first traces of such brine (liquid salt solution) with magnesium perchlorate as the main component were found on Mars in 2015, and in 2018, a reservoir with a diameter of about 20 kilometers was found under the polar ice of the planet, which could have been formed due to volcanic activity.  Later, planetary scientists confirmed that such lakes on Mars really exist and can be numerous.  Now Pralay Gayen (Pralay Gayen) from the University of Washington in St. Louis together with colleagues created an installation for obtaining oxygen and hydrogen from a saline solution close in composition and temperature to that in Martian lakes.  As a brine in the experiment, a solution of magnesium perchlorate in water with a concentration of 2.8 mol per liter was used, cooled to minus 36 degrees Celsius and blown by carbon dioxide (the latter played the role of the Martian atmosphere).  As an electrocatalyst for the production of oxygen, the scientists used lead-ruthenium oxide Pb2Ru2O7-δ, the effectiveness of which they previously showed for alkaline solutions.  The electrocatalyst for hydrogen production was platinum on activated carbon - the standard catalyst in this case, and a commercially produced anion-exchange membrane was used as a separator.  Installation diagram.  In the red region, oxygen is produced, in the blue - hydrogen.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS In the course of the study, scientists showed that lead-ruthenium oxide as an electrocatalyst is indeed several times more effective than the ruthenium oxide commonly used in such installations.  After the behavior of the created installation was studied in a wide range of temperatures from − 36 to 21 degrees Celsius and saw no radical fluctuations in the efficiency and rate of production.  The current output of the experimental installation was 70 percent, and the energy efficiency was in the range between 36 and 70 percent (depending on the voltage applied to the plates).  In addition, the installation was resistant to degradation of the catalyst: scientists were not able to find traces of ruthenium in the solution after 300-minute operation of the device.  The rate of production of oxygen (blue dots) and hydrogen (red dots), depending on the density of the cathode current.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS Also, the researchers compared the achieved rate of oxygen production with MOXIE values of 10-22 grams per hour: it turned out that with the same energy supply, the created installation produces 25 times more oxygen than the experiment on the Mars Rover “Perseverance ”.  To have the same rate of oxygen production as MOXIE, the device would have to have electrodes with an area of ​ ​ 28-62 square centimeters, and to ensure the vital activity of a sleeping and actively moving person, this parameter would have to be 375 and 1235 square centimeters, respectively.  At the same time, the mass and volume of the installation will be less than if you use the technology inherent in MOXIE.  Moreover, the developed method of obtaining oxygen does not require its subsequent purification, while during electrolysis in MOXIE, carbon monoxide is also produced, which must be filtered.  Dependence on the power consumption of the rate of oxygen production of the installation (blue line), as well as its capes and volume to ensure various modes of human life (black lines).  The blue dot is the power and rate of oxygen production at MOXIE.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS Previously, we talked about another method of obtaining oxygen from carbon dioxide in the Martian atmosphere (like MOXIE): scientists proposed to do this using low-temperature plasma.  And what is the role of the Mars Rover “Perseverance ” in addition to checking the method of oxygen production, you can read in our material“ Mars, there and back ”.  Nikita Kozyrev

Title: New technology will be able to produce hydrogen and oxygen from salty Martian water
Content: In space launches, weight matters a lot, so the less we have to take with us, the better.  Now engineers at St. Louis University have developed a new electrolysis device that can convert very salty Martian water into breathable oxygen and hydrogen for fuel. These gases can then be collected for use, so in theory electrolysis could be a way for astronauts to produce their own oxygen and hydrogen on the Red Planet.  The problem is that it doesn ’ t work well with brackish water, and that ’ s all you can find on Mars.  First, it is necessary to reduce the high salt content, which is a complex process in this inhospitable alien environment.  Therefore, for the new study, scientists have developed a new electrolysis system that can work with salt water in the extreme cold of the Martian atmosphere.  The key change is in two electrodes: the team created an anode from lead ruthenate pyrochlor and a cathode from platinum on the coal. Title: How does NASA build a base with breathable air on Mars?
Content: The purpose of writing this article is to understand how we can now prepare for human life on an alien planet, and to do so, Digital Trends spoke to two experts.  Michael Hackett, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Assad Abu Bakr, a NASA engineer, talk about how to keep astronauts alive on a planet that wants to take their lives.  The window of opportunity to send humans to the Red Planet has to pass some kind of necessary timeframe.  Because of the structure of the orbits of Earth and Mars, the easiest way to get from one planet to another is to use the Hohmann Transport Orbit, in which the spacecraft moves in an elliptical orbit and slowly and steadily pushes out.  Hackett explains, “It ’ s because of the way the planets move.  Earth is in orbit around Mars and is moving faster than Mars, so every once in a while they collide.  A year on Mars equals about two years on Earth. ”  So you have to go with the exact timing to launch astronauts to Mars.  Every Martian year, or every 26 months on Earth, is given a window of opportunity at which Mars is closest to Earth.  "So you have an optimal opportunity every 26 months to send a spacecraft to Mars through this orbit.  “So the plans for Mars are to send the infrastructure first, and then after 26 months, we ’ ll send the crew. ”  Sending infrastructure doesn ’ t just mean ensuring astronauts have access to air to breathe and food to eat.  It also means sending and building power plants, a habitat, rovers, and vehicles that will allow astronauts to leave Mars once the mission is complete.  Why is oxygen so important?  The first major problem to deal with when building a Martian base is the production of oxygen.  When you hear about producing oxygen on Mars, you ’ re probably thinking about the simplest human need: having air to breathe, and certainly not finding a way to produce a breathable atmosphere inside a confined habitat on Mars.  But the habitat will require, at least compared to other components of the project, very small amounts of oxygen.  By other components, we mean things like rocket propellants that lift astronauts off the surface of the planet.  Hackett explains, “We are trying to manufacture the drive prerequisites.  "We're not trying to make fuel, we're trying to get some of the necessary chemical reactions that we never think about on Earth."  On the ground, when you burn gasoline in your car ’ s engine, you use oxygen that weighs several times more than your fuel to cause that reaction.  The same is true of pieces of wood burning in the fireplace.  “But if you go somewhere where there is no free oxygen, you have to take oxygen with you. ”  Modern missiles have several liquid oxygen tanks that provide the final fuel and add a lot of weight to the entire payload.  “We ’ ll need about 30 tons of oxygen to get those astronauts off the surface and into orbit, and if we have to take those 30 tons of oxygen with us to Mars, the whole mission will be delayed for about a decade.  A much easier solution would be to send an empty tank there and fill it with oxygen. ”  Using what is available to produce oxygen on Mars, Hackett and his colleagues are working on a concept called In-situ Resource Utilization (ISRU).  Basically, it means using whatever is already found on Mars to build what we need.  They will have to experiment with a device called MOXIE, which, along with NASA's Endurance rover, successfully landed on Mars in February 2021.  MOXIE is essentially a miniature version of a much larger device that picks up carbon dioxide, which is found abundantly in the Martian atmosphere, and produces oxygen.  This device may seem complicated at first glance, but it ’ s actually similar to a very well-known technology on the planet.  According to Hackett, “MOXIE is very much like a fuel cell.  There is basically no difference between the two.  If you take a fuel cell and you reverse the two wires that have been wired into it, you have an electrification system.  This means that if the device is a fuel cell, you have a fuel and an oxidizer that deliver a stable molecule.  If you have carbon monoxide as fuel and oxygen, carbon dioxide is produced.  You also get electricity. ”  “Now, if you reverse that, you have to let in carbon dioxide and electricity, and what you get is carbon monoxide and oxygen.  That ’ s how we ’ ll solve the problem. ”  This seemingly simple idea is radical in that it addresses a problem that no one outside the aerospace community sees as a challenge: producing oxygen.  Hackett said, “Nobody wants to produce oxygen on Earth.  No one has a reason to do that.  Oxygen is everywhere. ”  How to build an oxygen machine?  Understanding the chemical rules of making an oxygen machine is one thing, and designing and implementing a version of it that fits inside a rover is another.  Abu Bakr, the MOXIE thermal engineer at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and who has been involved in the development of the MOXIE project from the beginning, explains how the experimental device was built and what obstacles the NASA lab team had to overcome.  He said: “The biggest challenge we ’ ve ever had is a little bit of energy.  The rover has a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, which is a nuclear source of electricity, so people think the rover relies on nuclear power, but that's not the case.  The rover is powered by batteries and has an atomic charger next to it. ”  This means that researchers need to be very careful about how much energy is being used to keep the battery from draining.  The entire Mars Endurance operates at only 110 watts, which is just a little more energy than it takes to light a light-bulb bulb.  As a result, a device like MOXIE has to operate with very small amounts of energy.  Simple knowledge but equipment design is only one aspect of trial and error – the other is to see if the idea works at all on Mars.  Even with concepts that work well on Earth, an alien environment can have unforeseen consequences, from the impact of the planet ’ s thin atmosphere on how heat is transferred to the depreciation of equipment in unexpected ways due to weaker gravity and unknown dust.  That ’ s why NASA engineers will soon be collecting MOXIE data to test its performance in Mars ’ true environment.  “In many ways, ” says Abu Bakr,“ MOXIE doesn ’ t really collect scientific data. ”  Compared to scientific equipment such as telescopes and spectrometers used to analyze rock samples, the data collected by MOXIE is relatively simple.  “What we get is almost like telemetry data in engineering.  We measure voltages and currents and temperatures, things like that.  This is our data, and the data is very small.  You can almost fit all of them in a floppy disk. ”  This means the team can get very quick feedback on whether the system is working properly – in just a few days.  Unlike other instruments on the endurance rover, which require weeks, months, or even years to analyze the data, MOXIE is a demonstration of practical performance rather than trial and error.  Abu Bakr said, “What we ’ re doing is not science, it ’ s technology.  We want to know whether the system works, and if we want to increase the scale in the future, what we need to do to make our goal work. ”  If MOXIE is successful, it will show how practical the ISRU principle is on Mars.  Then expanding the scale of the project and building a version of the machine on a real scale that produces oxygen at a much higher rate will be relatively easy; and the good news is that a larger version will appear more efficient and produce significant amounts of oxygen without requiring much energy.  With the oxygen challenge solved, we could move on to other resources humans need to survive on Mars.  Another essential resource that we need to establish in order to produce it on the Red Planet is water.  Water isn ’ t just necessary for humans to drink, but it ’ s also important because of the hydrogen and carbon dioxide compounds that can bring a plethora of efficient chemical compounds.  Hackett said: “The idea in the short term is to automate certain amounts of ISRU to make our mission possible.  “Once we build our base on Mars — a base like the McMurdo Station in Antarctica or the International Space Station — we can move on to more sophisticated ISRU methods like ice extraction. ”  “A lot of people feel like we need to extract ice automatically.  But I say no, it ’ s not worth the effort.  Ice is a mineral, which means you have to look for it underground, dig it out of the ground, and purify it.  It would be easier to take ice with us to Mars.  It's like a moxie, but it's a mechanical tree.  It breathes carbon dioxide and exhales oxygen. ”  Hackett argues that MOXIE is much easier to find resources through mining.  “It doesn ’ t have to go anywhere, it doesn ’ t have to look for anything.  These are methods in IRSU that appear to be really practical in the short term.  “You ’ re doing things as simple as possible, and one day you ’ ll have access to enough people

Title: Earth ’ s microbes should be sent to Mars.
Content: Space agencies have taken a lot of precautions not to contaminate celestial bodies with terrestrial microbes, but some researchers believe sending Earth microbes to Mars could be beneficial because doing so could transform the Martian environment into a habitat for humans.  Researchers have recently said that Earth ’ s microbes should be sent to Mars for colonization so that the Red Planet becomes a suitable place for humans to live.  A recent study has shown that the spread of Earth ’ s microbes could trigger a change in the structure of the Red Planet and create an environment where humans can live.  Scientists have developed a process that involves screening promising microbes and leaving the most important on Mars.  The researchers' new paper shows that the release of human microbes is the beginning of the process of restructuring the Red Planet and creating an environment in which humans can inhabit.  Jose Lopez, a microbiologist and professor at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, USA, conducted the study with his colleagues.  They asked NASA and other space agencies to send microbes to Mars so they could change the planet ’ s unpredictable environment and create a habitable environment on Mars.  The main argument of the researchers is that preventing pollution is nearly impossible, but it can be done by doing some things, such as sending human microbes there.  According to the researchers, microorganisms are what made our planet habitable.  As we know, without beneficial microorganisms, life cannot exist.  More than four billion years ago, Earth was not a habitable place, but microbial life arose and evolved over time.  The findings were published in the FEMS Journal of Microbiology Ecology.

Title: Scientists have found organisms that can give rise to life on Mars
Content: Scientists have found organisms that can give rise to life on Mars 16.02.2021, 14: 58 They are able to grow and multiply in the conditions of the red planet.  New experiments have shown that cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, can successfully grow in Martian atmospheric conditions.  Of course, a few more ingredients will be needed, but when humans get to Mars, they will be able to create life support systems based on cyanobacteria for the human habitat, writes nv.ua.  "Here we show that cyanobacteria can use the gases available in the Martian atmosphere, at low overall pressure, as a source of carbon and nitrogen," said astrobiologist Cyprien Verso from the University of Bremen in Germany.  "Under these conditions, cyanobacteria retained their ability to grow in water containing only Martian dust, and they could be used to feed other microbes.  This can help make long-term missions to Mars sustainable, ” the authors of the study believe.  All types of cyanobacteria produce oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis, and even today they are an invaluable source of it.  For several years, scientists have speculated whether we could use the ability of cyanobacteria to produce oxygen to live on Mars.  This will bring additional benefits.  The atmosphere of Mars consists mainly of carbon dioxide (95 percent) and nitrogen (3 percent), which are fixed by cyanobacteria, turning them into organic compounds and nutrients, respectively.  However, atmospheric pressure on Mars is a big problem.  The total pressure there is less than 1% of Earth ’ s — from 6 to 11 GPa: this is too small for the presence of liquid water, while the partial pressure of gaseous nitrogen — from 0.2 to 0.3 GPa — is not enough for their metabolism.  But recreating the atmosphere, like on Earth, would be too expensive: gases would have to be imported.  So the researchers were looking for a middle ground: an atmosphere close to Martian, which allows cyanobacteria to grow well.  The authors have developed a bioreactor called Atmos, which has an atmospheric pressure of about 10 percent of Earth ’ s, but uses only what can be found on Mars, albeit in inverted proportions: 96 percent nitrogen and 4 percent carbon dioxide.  The bioreactor also included water that can be obtained on Mars from melting ice, which in some places is abundant on the surface, and a simulator of Martian regolith, a mixture of minerals created here on Earth using only what can be found on Mars.  The team chose the type of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria that preliminary trials showed was most likely to thrive under these conditions, Anabaena sp.  PCC 7938, and tested it in a variety of conditions.  The researchers concluded that nitrogen-fixing, oxygen-producing cyanobacteria can be grown on Mars at low pressure under controlled conditions using exclusively local ingredients.  From cyanobacteria, sugar, amino acids and other nutrients can be obtained to feed other crops, which can then be used for other purposes, such as the production of medicines.  Atmos was designed to test whether cyanobacteria can be grown under certain atmospheric conditions rather than for maximum efficiency, and the parameters of the bioreactor will depend on many factors in the mission to Mars, including the payload and mission architecture.  However, now that the concept has been proven, the team can begin work on optimizing the bioreactor system that could one day save us life on Mars. Title: Oxygen and hydrogen on Mars proposed to get from brine
Content: Scientists have developed a method for producing oxygen and hydrogen from a liquid saline solution in Martian lakes using electrolysis.  A feature of the experiment was the use of lead-ruthenium oxide as an electrocatalyst for oxygen production.  The production of oxygen using such an installation was 25 times more energy efficient than in the case of MOXIE, launched to the Red Planet as part of the Mars 2020 mission, and the size and weight of the device for life support based on the described technology will be less than that of analogues.  The article was published in the journal PNAS.  Conditions on Mars are far from favorable for humans: the atmosphere is rarefied and 95 percent consists of carbon dioxide, and temperature changes exceed 100 degrees Celsius with an average temperature of minus 63 degrees.  Therefore, colonization of the Red Planet is impossible without the creation of a life support system that would be able to provide people with oxygen for breathing and fuel (for example, hydrogen) for energy supply and, ideally, return flight.  To solve the first problem, NASA created MOXIE (Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment) - an experimental installation for obtaining oxygen from atmospheric carbon dioxide by electrolysis.  To test the effectiveness of such a method in the field, the installation became part of the Mars Rover Perseverance, which was launched on July 30, 2020 as part of the Mars 2020 mission.  An alternative source of not only oxygen, but also hydrogen on Mars can be water, the first direct evidence of the existence of which on the red planet was obtained in 1971.  Particularly attractive for use in applications, however, would be the reserves of salt water, impurities in which would allow it to remain in a liquid state even at low temperature and pressure.  The first traces of such brine (liquid salt solution) with magnesium perchlorate as the main component were found on Mars in 2015, and in 2018, a reservoir with a diameter of about 20 kilometers was found under the polar ice of the planet, which could have been formed due to volcanic activity.  Later, planetary scientists confirmed that such lakes on Mars really exist and can be numerous.  Now Pralay Gayen (Pralay Gayen) from the University of Washington in St. Louis together with colleagues created an installation for obtaining oxygen and hydrogen from a saline solution close in composition and temperature to that in Martian lakes.  As a brine in the experiment, a solution of magnesium perchlorate in water with a concentration of 2.8 mol per liter was used, cooled to minus 36 degrees Celsius and blown by carbon dioxide (the latter played the role of the Martian atmosphere).  As an electrocatalyst for the production of oxygen, the scientists used lead-ruthenium oxide Pb2Ru2O7-δ, the effectiveness of which they previously showed for alkaline solutions.  The electrocatalyst for hydrogen production was platinum on activated carbon - the standard catalyst in this case, and a commercially produced anion-exchange membrane was used as a separator.  Installation diagram.  In the red region, oxygen is produced, in the blue - hydrogen.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS In the course of the study, scientists showed that lead-ruthenium oxide as an electrocatalyst is indeed several times more effective than the ruthenium oxide commonly used in such installations.  After the behavior of the created installation was studied in a wide range of temperatures from − 36 to 21 degrees Celsius and saw no radical fluctuations in the efficiency and rate of production.  The current output of the experimental installation was 70 percent, and the energy efficiency was in the range between 36 and 70 percent (depending on the voltage applied to the plates).  In addition, the installation was resistant to degradation of the catalyst: scientists were not able to find traces of ruthenium in the solution after 300-minute operation of the device.  The rate of production of oxygen (blue dots) and hydrogen (red dots), depending on the density of the cathode current.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS Also, the researchers compared the achieved rate of oxygen production with MOXIE values of 10-22 grams per hour: it turned out that with the same energy supply, the created installation produces 25 times more oxygen than the experiment on the Mars Rover “Perseverance ”.  To have the same rate of oxygen production as MOXIE, the device would have to have electrodes with an area of ​ ​ 28-62 square centimeters, and to ensure the vital activity of a sleeping and actively moving person, this parameter would have to be 375 and 1235 square centimeters, respectively.  At the same time, the mass and volume of the installation will be less than if you use the technology inherent in MOXIE.  Moreover, the developed method of obtaining oxygen does not require its subsequent purification, while during electrolysis in MOXIE, carbon monoxide is also produced, which must be filtered.  Dependence on the power consumption of the rate of oxygen production of the installation (blue line), as well as its capes and volume to ensure various modes of human life (black lines).  The blue dot is the power and rate of oxygen production at MOXIE.  Image source: Pralay Gayen et al. / PNAS Previously, we talked about another method of obtaining oxygen from carbon dioxide in the Martian atmosphere (like MOXIE): scientists proposed to do this using low-temperature plasma.  And what is the role of the Mars Rover “Perseverance ” in addition to checking the method of oxygen production, you can read in our material“ Mars, there and back ”.  Nikita Kozyrev

The window of opportunity to send humans to the Red Planet has to pass some kind of necessary timeframe.  Because of the structure of the orbits of Earth and Mars, the easiest way to get from one planet to another is to use the Hohmann Transport Orbit, in which the spacecraft moves in an elliptical orbit and slowly and steadily pushes out.  Hackett explains, “It ’ s because of the way the planets move.  Earth is in orbit around Mars and is moving faster than Mars, so every once in a while they collide.  A year on Mars equals about two years on Earth. ”  So you have to go with the exact timing to launch astronauts to Mars.  Every Martian year, or every 26 months on Earth, is given a window of opportunity at which Mars is closest to Earth.  "So you have an optimal opportunity every 26 months to send a spacecraft to Mars through this orbit.  “So the plans for Mars are to send the infrastructure first, and then after 26 months, we ’ ll send the crew. ”  Sending infrastructure doesn ’ t just mean ensuring astronauts have access to air to breathe and food to eat.  It also means sending and building power plants, a habitat, rovers, and vehicles that will allow astronauts to leave Mars once the mission is complete.  Why is oxygen so important?  The first major problem to deal with when building a Martian base is the production of oxygen.  When you hear about producing oxygen on Mars, you ’ re probably thinking about the simplest human need: having air to breathe, and certainly not finding a way to produce a breathable atmosphere inside a confined habitat on Mars.  But the habitat will require, at least compared to other components of the project, very small amounts of oxygen.  By other components, we mean things like rocket propellants that lift astronauts off the surface of the planet.  Hackett explains, “We are trying to manufacture the drive prerequisites.  "We're not trying to make fuel, we're trying to get some of the necessary chemical reactions that we never think about on Earth."  On the ground, when you burn gasoline in your car ’ s engine, you use oxygen that weighs several times more than your fuel to cause that reaction.  The same is true of pieces of wood burning in the fireplace.  “But if you go somewhere where there is no free oxygen, you have to take oxygen with you. ”  Modern missiles have several liquid oxygen tanks that provide the final fuel and add a lot of weight to the entire payload.  “We ’ ll need about 30 tons of oxygen to get those astronauts off the surface and into orbit, and if we have to take those 30 tons of oxygen with us to Mars, the whole mission will be delayed for about a decade.  A much easier solution would be to send an empty tank there and fill it with oxygen. ”  Using what is available to produce oxygen on Mars, Hackett and his colleagues are working on a concept called In-situ Resource Utilization (ISRU).  Basically, it means using whatever is already found on Mars to build what we need.  They will have to experiment with a device called MOXIE, which, along with NASA's Endurance rover, successfully landed on Mars in February 2021.  MOXIE is essentially a miniature version of a much larger device that picks up carbon dioxide, which is found abundantly in the Martian atmosphere, and produces oxygen.  This device may seem complicated at first glance, but it ’ s actually similar to a very well-known technology on the planet.  According to Hackett, “MOXIE is very much like a fuel cell.  There is basically no difference between the two.  If you take a fuel cell and you reverse the two wires that have been wired into it, you have an electrification system.  This means that if the device is a fuel cell, you have a fuel and an oxidizer that deliver a stable molecule.  If you have carbon monoxide as fuel and oxygen, carbon dioxide is produced.  You also get electricity. ”  “Now, if you reverse that, you have to let in carbon dioxide and electricity, and what you get is carbon monoxide and oxygen.  That ’ s how we ’ ll solve the problem. ”  This seemingly simple idea is radical in that it addresses a problem that no one outside the aerospace community sees as a challenge: producing oxygen.  Hackett said, “Nobody wants to produce oxygen on Earth.  No one has a reason to do that.  Oxygen is everywhere. ”  How to build an oxygen machine?  Understanding the chemical rules of making an oxygen machine is one thing, and designing and implementing a version of it that fits inside a rover is another.  Abu Bakr, the MOXIE thermal engineer at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and who has been involved in the development of the MOXIE project from the beginning, explains how the experimental device was built and what obstacles the NASA lab team had to overcome.  He said: “The biggest challenge we ’ ve ever had is a little bit of energy.  The rover has a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, which is a nuclear source of electricity, so people think the rover relies on nuclear power, but that's not the case.  The rover is powered by batteries and has an atomic charger next to it. ”  This means that researchers need to be very careful about how much energy is being used to keep the battery from draining.  The entire Mars Endurance operates at only 110 watts, which is just a little more energy than it takes to light a light-bulb bulb.  As a result, a device like MOXIE has to operate with very small amounts of energy.  Simple knowledge but equipment design is only one aspect of trial and error – the other is to see if the idea works at all on Mars.  Even with concepts that work well on Earth, an alien environment can have unforeseen consequences, from the impact of the planet ’ s thin atmosphere on how heat is transferred to the depreciation of equipment in unexpected ways due to weaker gravity and unknown dust.  That ’ s why NASA engineers will soon be collecting MOXIE data to test its performance in Mars ’ true environment.  “In many ways, ” says Abu Bakr,“ MOXIE doesn ’ t really collect scientific data. ”  Compared to scientific equipment such as telescopes and spectrometers used to analyze rock samples, the data collected by MOXIE is relatively simple.  “What we get is almost like telemetry data in engineering.  We measure voltages and currents and temperatures, things like that.  This is our data, and the data is very small.  You can almost fit all of them in a floppy disk. ”  This means the team can get very quick feedback on whether the system is working properly – in just a few days.  Unlike other instruments on the endurance rover, which require weeks, months, or even years to analyze the data, MOXIE is a demonstration of practical performance rather than trial and error.  Abu Bakr said, “What we ’ re doing is not science, it ’ s technology.  We want to know whether the system works, and if we want to increase the scale in the future, what we need to do to make our goal work. ”  If MOXIE is successful, it will show how practical the ISRU principle is on Mars.  Then expanding the scale of the project and building a version of the machine on a real scale that produces oxygen at a much higher rate will be relatively easy; and the good news is that a larger version will appear more efficient and produce significant amounts of oxygen without requiring much energy.  With the oxygen challenge solved, we could move on to other resources humans need to survive on Mars.  Another essential resource that we need to establish in order to produce it on the Red Planet is water.  Water isn ’ t just necessary for humans to drink, but it ’ s also important because of the hydrogen and carbon dioxide compounds that can bring a plethora of efficient chemical compounds.  Hackett said: “The idea in the short term is to automate certain amounts of ISRU to make our mission possible.  “Once we build our base on Mars — a base like the McMurdo Station in Antarctica or the International Space Station — we can move on to more sophisticated ISRU methods like ice extraction. ”  “A lot of people feel like we need to extract ice automatically.  But I say no, it ’ s not worth the effort.  Ice is a mineral, which means you have to look for it underground, dig it out of the ground, and purify it.  It would be easier to take ice with us to Mars.  It's like a moxie, but it's a mechanical tree.  It breathes carbon dioxide and exhales oxygen. ”  Hackett argues that MOXIE is much easier to find resources through mining.  “It doesn ’ t have to go anywhere, it doesn ’ t have to look for anything.
