Title: Earth ’ s microbes should be sent to Mars.
Content: Space agencies have taken a lot of precautions not to contaminate celestial bodies with terrestrial microbes, but some researchers believe sending Earth microbes to Mars could be beneficial because doing so could transform the Martian environment into a habitat for humans.  Researchers have recently said that Earth ’ s microbes should be sent to Mars for colonization so that the Red Planet becomes a suitable place for humans to live.  A recent study has shown that the spread of Earth ’ s microbes could trigger a change in the structure of the Red Planet and create an environment where humans can live.  Scientists have developed a process that involves screening promising microbes and leaving the most important on Mars.  The researchers' new paper shows that the release of human microbes is the beginning of the process of restructuring the Red Planet and creating an environment in which humans can inhabit.  Jose Lopez, a microbiologist and professor at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, USA, conducted the study with his colleagues.  They asked NASA and other space agencies to send microbes to Mars so they could change the planet ’ s unpredictable environment and create a habitable environment on Mars.  The main argument of the researchers is that preventing pollution is nearly impossible, but it can be done by doing some things, such as sending human microbes there.  According to the researchers, microorganisms are what made our planet habitable.  As we know, without beneficial microorganisms, life cannot exist.  More than four billion years ago, Earth was not a habitable place, but microbial life arose and evolved over time.  The findings were published in the FEMS Journal of Microbiology Ecology.

Title: Scientists have found organisms that can give rise to life on Mars
Content: Scientists have found organisms that can give rise to life on Mars 16.02.2021, 14: 58 They are able to grow and multiply in the conditions of the red planet.  New experiments have shown that cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, can successfully grow in Martian atmospheric conditions.  Of course, a few more ingredients will be needed, but when humans get to Mars, they will be able to create life support systems based on cyanobacteria for the human habitat, writes nv.ua.  "Here we show that cyanobacteria can use the gases available in the Martian atmosphere, at low overall pressure, as a source of carbon and nitrogen," said astrobiologist Cyprien Verso from the University of Bremen in Germany.  "Under these conditions, cyanobacteria retained their ability to grow in water containing only Martian dust, and they could be used to feed other microbes.  This can help make long-term missions to Mars sustainable, ” the authors of the study believe.  All types of cyanobacteria produce oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis, and even today they are an invaluable source of it.  For several years, scientists have speculated whether we could use the ability of cyanobacteria to produce oxygen to live on Mars.  This will bring additional benefits.  The atmosphere of Mars consists mainly of carbon dioxide (95 percent) and nitrogen (3 percent), which are fixed by cyanobacteria, turning them into organic compounds and nutrients, respectively.  However, atmospheric pressure on Mars is a big problem.  The total pressure there is less than 1% of Earth ’ s — from 6 to 11 GPa: this is too small for the presence of liquid water, while the partial pressure of gaseous nitrogen — from 0.2 to 0.3 GPa — is not enough for their metabolism.  But recreating the atmosphere, like on Earth, would be too expensive: gases would have to be imported.  So the researchers were looking for a middle ground: an atmosphere close to Martian, which allows cyanobacteria to grow well.  The authors have developed a bioreactor called Atmos, which has an atmospheric pressure of about 10 percent of Earth ’ s, but uses only what can be found on Mars, albeit in inverted proportions: 96 percent nitrogen and 4 percent carbon dioxide.  The bioreactor also included water that can be obtained on Mars from melting ice, which in some places is abundant on the surface, and a simulator of Martian regolith, a mixture of minerals created here on Earth using only what can be found on Mars.  The team chose the type of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria that preliminary trials showed was most likely to thrive under these conditions, Anabaena sp.  PCC 7938, and tested it in a variety of conditions.  The researchers concluded that nitrogen-fixing, oxygen-producing cyanobacteria can be grown on Mars at low pressure under controlled conditions using exclusively local ingredients.  From cyanobacteria, sugar, amino acids and other nutrients can be obtained to feed other crops, which can then be used for other purposes, such as the production of medicines.  Atmos was designed to test whether cyanobacteria can be grown under certain atmospheric conditions rather than for maximum efficiency, and the parameters of the bioreactor will depend on many factors in the mission to Mars, including the payload and mission architecture.  However, now that the concept has been proven, the team can begin work on optimizing the bioreactor system that could one day save us life on Mars.
